young.html: What is the difference between a living thing and a rock? Aristotle's answer is the soul. But he does not mean a ghost inside the body. For Aristotle, the soul is simply what makes a body alive and able to do what living things do.

He noticed that living things can do different things. Plants take in food, grow and make seeds. Animals do all that, and they also feel: they see, hear, smell, taste or touch, and they want things and move toward them. People do all of that, and they can also think: ask why, do math, and plan.

young.name: gb-soul-powers
young.cap: Choose a plant, an animal or a person and see which powers it has.

young.html: Aristotle gave a picture to explain it: if your eye were a whole creature, seeing would be its soul. A painted eye or a stone eye looks like an eye, but it can't see, so it isn't really an eye at all.

Living-things sort. Make three columns: Plants, Animals, People. Go outside or look through a book and list ten living things. For each one, check off: Does it take in food and grow? Does it sense things? Does it move from place to place? Does it think and talk? Do your findings agree with Aristotle's? Are there any puzzling cases (like a sponge or a coral)?

full.html: On the Soul (Greek Peri Psychēs, Latin De Anima), from Aristotle's teaching years in Athens (about 335–322 BC), is the first book devoted to the study of life and mind. The Great Books set pairs it with his short works on sense, memory, sleep and dreams. Book I reviews earlier thinkers, who said the soul was made of fire, or air, or atoms, or was a harmony. Book II gives Aristotle's own definition, using his ideas of form and matter:

full.text: If then we were obliged to give a general description applicable to all soul or life, we should say that it is the first entelechy of a natural organic body. It is therefore unnecessary to ask whether body and soul are one, as one should not ask whether the wax and the figure are one…
full.author: Aristotle

full.html: Entelechy (Greek entelecheia) means actuality, being fully at work. A living body has the potential for life; its soul is that potential made actual. So soul and body are not two things glued together, any more than a seal's shape and the wax that carries it.

full.text: For if the eye were an animal, vision would be its soul, i.e. vision is the notional essence of the eye. The eye, however, is the matter of vision, and if the vision be wanting the eye is no longer an eye, save in the meaning of a homonym, as a stone eye or a painted eye.
full.author: Aristotle

full.html: Souls differ by their powers, which come in a ladder: each higher one needs the ones below it.

full.name: gb-soul-powers
full.cap: The ladder of powers. Every animal has at least touch; only human beings think, in Aristotle's account.

full.html: Aristotle explains sensing as taking in an object's form without its matter:

full.text: In reference to sensation in general we must understand that a sense is capable of receiving into itself sensible forms without their matter, just as wax receives into itself the mark of a ring without its iron or gold…
full.author: Aristotle

full.html: He studies each of the five senses and its medium: sight needs light through air or water; hearing, air set moving; touch, the flesh. Then he asks how we put the senses together, knowing that the yellow thing is also the sweet thing, and how we perceive things several senses share, such as size, shape, number and motion. He calls the power that does this the common sense (which is not the modern “good sense”). He also describes imagination (phantasia), the power to call up images when the object is not there.

Thinking, Aristotle says, is like sensing in that the mind takes on the form of what it thinks about. Before it thinks, the mind is like a tablet with nothing yet written on it. In a short and famous chapter (III.5) he adds that there is also a mind that makes things understood, as light makes colors visible, and calls it separable and undying. What he meant is one of the most argued-over questions in the history of philosophy.

items: On Memory and Recollection: memory is of the past and works through images; recollecting is searching, moving from one thought to the next by likeness, opposites or what came together, as when you retrace your steps.
On Sleep and On Dreams: dreams come from the movements the senses leave behind, like ripples after a stone, which we notice when the outside world goes quiet.
On Prophecy in Sleep: Aristotle is doubtful that dreams foretell the future, and says most seeming prophecies are coincidence.

full.html: Reading “soul” here as only the religious sense of the word. Aristotle's psychē covers the life of plants, animals and people, and his book is as much about biology and the mind as about religion. Readers have long discussed how his view of the mind relates to belief in life after death.

deep.html: Plato's Phaedo treats the soul as a separate being that can exist without the body. Aristotle's soul is the form of the living body, which is why it is much harder, on his view, to say that a person's soul outlives the body, except perhaps for the mind of III.5. Medieval thinkers took this up: Thomas Aquinas, later on this ladder, used Aristotle's definition and argued that the human soul is both the body's form and able to survive it, while other readers gave III.5 different meanings.

Modern biology and psychology study what Aristotle called the soul's powers: growth, sensation, memory, imagination and thought. Some philosophers of mind today describe their view as close to Aristotle's, treating the mind as what a living body does rather than as a separate thing.

items: Is a plant alive in the same way you are? What is the difference?
If a robot could see and move, would it have the second power of soul? What would Aristotle ask?
Why do dreams feel so real when the world around us is quiet?

questions: What makes something alive? Try to give an answer that works for a tree, a dog and a person.
Aristotle says a painted eye isn't really an eye because it can't see. Can you think of other things that are only “eyes in name”?
How do you remember where you left something? Do you “retrace your steps” the way Aristotle describes?
Which of your senses would be hardest to live without? Aristotle thought touch was the most necessary for animals. Why might that be?
Do you think animals can think? What would count as evidence?
